extracted.intended_audience: general literate coffee-house readers / 18th-century periodical audience
extracted.subtask_short: spectator essays on clubs and beauty
extracted.subtask_description: Short essays and moral reflections (The Spectator) describing social clubs, theatrical projects, and norms of beauty and conduct; includes anecdotal rules, maxims, and satire about suitable behavior and taste. Intended as public moral/social commentary rather than a formal guideline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission requirement to the Amorous Club
rubrics_metrics.description: A Mistress, and a Poem in her Praise, will introduce any Candidate: Without the latter no one can be admitted; for he that is not in love enough to rhime, is unqualified for our Society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership demands both declaration of a beloved and a poetic expression in her praise; the poem is a formal prerequisite and functions as proof of suitable passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on disparaging women (Amorous Club rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: To speak disrespectfully of any Woman, is Expulsion from our gentle Society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disrespect toward women is a ground for immediate removal; the club enforces polite and laudatory discourse as a membership standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance norms of the Amorous Club (behavioral expectations)
rubrics_metrics.description: We look upon a Man as no Company, that does not sigh five times in a Quarter of an Hour; and look upon a Member as very absurd, that is so much himself as to make a direct Answer to a Question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members are expected to adopt the theatrical mannerisms of lovers (sighing, absent-mindedness, playing with tokens) and to perform their passion rather than engage in straightforward, practical conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidency chosen by intensity of passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Our Presidentship is bestow'd according to the Dignity of Passion; ... In this Case, if any Man has declared the Violence of his Flame in more pathetick Terms, he is made President for that Night, out of respect to his superior Passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leadership within the club is awarded on the rhetorical/performative measure of expressed passion — more pathetic, eloquent expressions of love win symbolic authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy and internal constitution of the Amorous Club
rubrics_metrics.description: The Reason that we are so little known in the World, is the Secrecy which we are obliged to live under in the University. Our Constitution runs counter to that of the Place wherein we live: ... our Statutes are like those of the Druids, recorded in our own Breasts only, and explained by the Majority of the Company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The club privileges internal, oral statutes and secrecy; governance and interpretation are collective and informal rather than written or public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical rule: use of antiquated 'rules of love' to settle disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: As we are at present all of us Gown-men, instead of duelling when we are Rivals, we drink together the Health of our Mistress. The Manner of doing this sometimes indeed creates Debates; on such Occasions we have Recourse to the Rules of Love among the Antients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflicts among lovers are resolved ceremonially (toasts, classical precedents) rather than by violence; the passage models playful recourse to classical authority as conflict procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: nothing laudable that is not concerned with the will (Ugly-Club ethos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing ought to be laudable in a Man, in which his Will is not concerned; therefore our Society can follow Nature, and where she has thought fit, as it were, to mock herself, we can do so too, and be merry upon the Occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The club's moral is to avoid praising unearned natural attributes (e.g., inherited beauty); value is given to qualities shaped by will/agency rather than mere nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxim: features alone do not make beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: That no Woman can be Handsome by the Force of Features alone, any more than she can be Witty only by the Help of Speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True beauty requires more than favorable physical features; inner qualities and accomplishments contribute essentially to being regarded as handsome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: pride and affectation spoil beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: That Pride destroys all Symmetry and Grace, and Affectation is a more terrible Enemy to fine Faces than the Small-Pox.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pride and artificial affectation undermine natural grace and attractiveness — moral failings are aesthetic defects. Avoiding vanity and affectation is advised to preserve beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxim (original wording): relationship of beauty and falseness
rubrics_metrics.description: That no Woman is capable of being Beautiful, who is not incapable of being False.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a preliminary maxim; in context the author links truthfulness/virtue with authentic beauty (the phrasing is rhetorical and normative rather than a technical rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral criterion: what is odious in a friend is deformity in a mistress
rubrics_metrics.description: And, That what would be Odious in a Friend, is Deformity in a Mistress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traits tolerable or pardonable in private friends become disqualifying faults in a beloved or partner; standards for intimate partners are stricter regarding moral character and behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for improving beauty: cultivate virtuous qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: The true Art of assisting Beauty consists in Embellishing the whole Person by the proper Ornaments of virtuous and commendable Qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice: rather than relying on cosmetic quackery, one should cultivate character (innocence, piety, good humour, truth) and accomplishments to enhance attractiveness; inner virtues give enduring radiance to outward looks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice for the less naturally beautiful: acquire accomplishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Daphne ... found her self obliged to acquire some Accomplishments to make up for the want of those Attractions which she saw in her Sister.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those without striking natural beauty are advised to develop accomplishments, good sense, and agreeable behavior to gain esteem and attentions; social skills and merit can substitute for looks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between superficial cosmetics and true effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Colours, artfully spread upon Canvas, may entertain the Eye, but not affect the Heart; and she, who takes no care to add to the natural Graces of her Person any excelling Qualities, may be allowed still to amuse, as a Picture, but not to triumph as a Beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cosmetic or surface enhancements may please visually but will not touch the heart; lasting beauty arises from character, not mere ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of theatrical entertainments to subject and venue (satirical criticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some at the Table urged that a Puppet-Show was not a suitable Entertainment for Alexander the Great; and that it might be introduced more properly, if we suppose the Conqueror touched upon that part of India which is said to be inhabited by the Pigmies. But this Objection was looked upon as frivolous, and the Proposal immediately over-ruled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit criterion for dramatic production: entertainments should be appropriate to their subject and plausible within the dramatic world, though the narrator satirically treats objections as frivolous — the exchange highlights considerations of suitability and anachronism in staging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical constraint: venue limits what can be staged
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bull-baiting only excepted, which cannot possibly be exhibited in the Theatre, by Reason of the Lowness of the Roof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical constraints of venue impose limits on what spectacles can be legitimately staged; producers must consider practical feasibility when designing entertainments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience comprehension and language accessibility (satirical point)
rubrics_metrics.description: It was his Intention that the whole Opera should be acted in that Language [Greek], which was a Tongue he was sure would wonderfully please the Ladies... because there are fewer of them who understand Greek than Italian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although delivered satirically, this implies a practical consideration for performances: language choice affects audience appreciation and may be chosen (even strategically) according to who understands it — accessibility matters.
